title: Case conceptualization (formulation)
body: A case conceptualization is the consultant's working explanation of what is happening for a client and why. It pulls together everything gathered in assessment: the reason for consulting, performance history and demands, strengths, health and self-care, injury, motivation and readiness for change, and cultural and contextual factors inside and outside the performance environment. It links these to the presenting concern and points toward goals and an intervention plan. A good formulation draws on several methods (interview, observation, questionnaires, stakeholder input, performance data), treats discrepancies between sources as information, and is held as a hypothesis. It is shared and refined with the client and revised as new data arrive. It should also flag when the picture suggests a concern outside the consultant's competence or scope, which calls for referral.
points: Integrates multi-source data, including life outside sport
Tentative and testable; refined collaboratively with the client
Disagreement between sources is a clue, not noise
Identifies when referral is needed
examNote: Expect vignettes where one source (often a coach's label) conflicts with others; the best answer integrates all the data into a tentative explanation rather than adopting one view.

title: Motivational interviewing: OARS and change talk
body: Motivational interviewing (MI) is a collaborative, person-centered way of talking with someone who is ambivalent about change. Its core skills are OARS: Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections, and Summaries. During assessment, MI helps the consultant gauge readiness and hear the client's own reasons for change. Change talk is the client's language in favor of change: desire ("I want..."), ability ("I could..."), reasons, need, and, later, commitment and taking steps. Sustain talk argues for staying the same. The consultant evokes and reflects change talk and responds to sustain talk with reflection rather than argument. A double-sided reflection that ends on the change side is a common tool. The "righting reflex," also called the "fixing reflex" (pushing, persuading, confronting, or jumping to fix) tends to increase resistance, especially with clients referred by a coach.
points: OARS: open questions, affirmations, reflections, summaries
Change talk: desire, ability, reasons, need, commitment
Respond to sustain talk with reflection, not argument
Avoid the righting reflex with reluctant or referred clients
examNote: A likely scenario asks for the best response to an ambivalent client or which statement is change talk; the key reflects or evokes the client's own motivation, never confronts.

title: Socratic questioning
body: Socratic questioning uses open, curious questions that help clients examine their own thoughts and reach their own conclusions instead of being told what to think. In assessment it shows what a belief is, how firmly it is held, and what evidence the client draws on, which feeds the formulation. Later it supports cognitive restructuring through guided discovery. Typical questions ask for evidence ("What have you seen happen when...?"), alternatives ("How else could you read that?"), consequences ("What does believing this do to your preparation?"), and perspective ("What would you tell a teammate?"). Socratic questioning is not the same as reassurance, lecturing, labeling a thought as "irrational," or asking closed yes/no questions. The rationale is that conclusions clients reach themselves are likely to feel more convincing.
points: Open, evidence-seeking, non-leading questions
Guided discovery: the client reaches the conclusion
Not reassurance, arguing, or lecturing
Useful in assessment for mapping beliefs
examNote: When asked which response "reflects Socratic questioning," pick the open question that invites the client to examine evidence, not the one that reassures or corrects.

title: Performance profiling
body: Performance profiling, developed by Butler and Hardy from personal construct theory, asks the performer to name the qualities (mental, physical, technical, tactical) they believe matter for top performance in their role. They then rate their current level on each, often alongside an ideal or target rating. The gaps show priorities in the performer's own terms, which builds awareness, ownership, and motivation for goal setting. It suits clients who resist standardized questionnaires or feel "handed a checklist," and it adapts to teams, positions, and non-sport performers. Coaches can rate the same qualities so perceptions can be compared and discussed. For evaluation, the performer re-rates the same qualities later and compares them with the baseline; this tracks perceived change and guides plan revisions.
points: Performer generates the qualities, then rates current vs. ideal
Builds awareness and ownership of goals
Coach ratings can be compared, not substituted
Re-rate the same profile over time to monitor progress
examNote: Choose profiling when the stem stresses the client's own view of what matters or buy-in; in Domain V, re-rate the same qualities against the baseline.

title: Selecting, administering, and debriefing questionnaires
body: Start with the question, then choose the instrument. Is the interest a state (how someone feels before this event) or a trait (a general tendency)? Does the instrument have validity and reliability evidence for this population, age, and language? Norms only apply to the groups they were built on, and ad hoc translations lack validity evidence. Obtain informed consent that says who will see the results and for what purpose. For minors, get guardian permission plus the minor's assent. Administer under consistent conditions: state measures depend on timing, and anonymity or confidential coding matters for team measures. Store data securely. Give feedback as a collaborative conversation that treats scores as hypotheses to check against the client's experience. Never base a decision on a single score, and never use results for purposes, such as selection, that the instrument and consent do not support. Clinical screeners may be used only with appropriate training, policy, and a referral pathway; they flag rather than diagnose.
points: Match state vs. trait to the question; check population, age, language
Consent defines who sees results and how they are used
Consistent administration; secure storage; anonymity or coding for team measures
Debrief collaboratively; never rely on one score
examNote: A likely scenario turns on appropriate use rather than the instrument itself: wrong population norms, a coach wanting individual scores, or a screener treated as a diagnosis.

title: Anxiety instruments: CSAI-2 and SAS-2
body: The Competitive State Anxiety Inventory-2 (CSAI-2) measures state cognitive anxiety, somatic anxiety, and self-confidence. It was built from multidimensional anxiety theory and is designed to be completed shortly before competition (traditionally about an hour before). Because it captures a moment, it is ideal for tracking pre-competition states across events. Comparisons are meaningful only when timing and the type of event are kept similar. Later work added directional scales asking whether symptoms feel facilitative or debilitative, and concerns about factor structure led to a revised form (CSAI-2R). The Sport Anxiety Scale-2 (SAS-2) measures trait sport performance anxiety: somatic anxiety, worry, and concentration disruption. It was developed for children as well as adults. Use it to describe a general tendency, such as an athlete who is nervous before every competition regardless of stakes, or as a pre/post measure of change in that tendency.
points: CSAI-2: state cognitive anxiety, somatic anxiety, self-confidence
CSAI-2 timing: close to competition; repeat under similar conditions
SAS-2: trait somatic anxiety, worry, concentration disruption
SAS-2 suits youth and adults
examNote: Decide state vs. trait from the stem ("right now, before this race" vs. "usually, across competitions") and check the client's age; then pick the CSAI-2 or the SAS-2.

title: Skills and attention inventories: TOPS, ACSI-28, TAIS
body: The Test of Performance Strategies (TOPS) measures how often athletes use psychological skills and strategies, with separate practice and competition sections. Practice-section scales include goal setting, imagery, self-talk, relaxation, activation, emotional control, automaticity, and attentional control; the competition section includes negative thinking. This makes it a good fit when performance differs between training and competition. The Athletic Coping Skills Inventory-28 (ACSI-28) gives a broad picture of psychological coping skills in sport, such as coping with adversity, peaking under pressure, concentration, confidence and achievement motivation, and coachability. It does not separate settings. The Test of Attentional and Interpersonal Style (TAIS), based on Nideffer's model, profiles attentional width (broad–narrow) and direction (internal–external), including overload tendencies, plus interpersonal style. Choose it when the question is the type of attention, not just how well someone concentrates. Interpret it cautiously, because evidence for its factor structure and validity is mixed.
points: TOPS: skill use, separately for practice and competition
ACSI-28: broad sport coping skills profile
TAIS: attentional width/direction and overload, plus interpersonal style
ACSI-28 concentration is not the same as attentional style
examNote: Practice-vs-competition gaps point to the TOPS; broad/narrow or internal/external attention problems point to the TAIS.

title: Other instruments, observation, and multi-source data
body: TEOSQ: task vs. ego goal orientation, that is, whether success is defined as improvement or as beating others. SIQ: how often imagery is used for cognitive and motivational functions (imagery use). MIQ-3: ease of generating external visual, internal visual, and kinesthetic movement images (imagery ability). AIMS: the strength and exclusivity of athletic identity, relevant to injury and transition. POMS: mood states; repeated monitoring can show responses to training load, such as an inverted "iceberg" with high fatigue and low vigor. Mood profiles flag issues; they do not diagnose overtraining. GEQ: task and social cohesion. Collect it anonymously and report at team level. Beyond questionnaires, systematic observation defines target behaviors, records them as they happen, and samples several contexts. Coach and stakeholder input (with consent) is most useful as specific, observable examples. Performance metrics, video, and wearables add objective data, but each measures something specific. Triangulate sources and explore disagreements with the client.
points: SIQ = imagery use; MIQ-3 = imagery ability
POMS trends flag possible overreaching; route to coaching and medical staff
GEQ: anonymous, aggregate reporting
Observation: defined behaviors, real-time records, multiple contexts
examNote: Expect instrument-matching vignettes and items on reassessing with the same method and conditions as the baseline, plus triangulation when sources disagree.
